Order:

This Criminal Petition is filed under Section 528 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS), seeking quashment of the proceedings dated 30.08.2023 in C.C. No.350 of 2017 on the file of the XII Additional Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, Hyderabad.

entities.text: XII Additional Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, Hyderabad
entities.label: COURT

sentences.text:
Brief Facts:
2.1.
The factual matrix, as borne out from the record, reveals that respondent Nos.2 to 6, who are the de facto complainants, lodged a complaint on 18.07.2013 before the Commissioner of Police, Hyderabad.

The gravamen of the allegations is that accused Nos.1 to 8 induced the complainants and several others to invest an aggregate sum of Rs.1,70,00,000/-, representing that low cost housing would be provided to economically weaker sections under certain governmental schemes.

2.2. Acting upon such representations, Crime No.108 of 2013 was registered for offences punishable under Sections 406 (criminal breach of trust), 420 (cheating), and 120-B (criminal conspiracy) of the Indian Penal Code.

2.3. As per the charge sheet, accused Nos.1 to 8 allegedly collected money from the public under the Smt. A Suneela vs State Of Telangana on 5 March, 2026 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/49731745/
1 guise of providing housing benefits.

entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: It is further alleged that accused Nos.1 and 2 approached the petitioner (arrayed as accused No.5) and requested her to exercise her influence to secure allotment of houses under the Indiramma Pakka Gruhalu Scheme, a welfare initiative intended for weaker sections.
2.4. The prosecution further alleges that certain amounts were routed to the petitioner through accused Nos.3 and 4 for the purpose of facilitating such allotments.

It is also alleged that accused Nos.3 and 4, relying upon the assurances attributed to the petitioner, collected funds from members of the public through voluntary organizations in the name of the S.C. Corporation and housing schemes for weaker sections, and that an amount of approximately Rs.9,50,000/- was paid in furtherance of the said arrangement.
2.5. During the course of investigation, statements of witnesses were recorded under Section 161 Cr.P.C.
Upon completion of the investigation, a charge sheet was filed on 28.04.2014 against accused Nos.1 to 8.
The learned Magistrate took cognizance of the offences and numbered the case as C.C. No.350 of 2017.
Aggrieved by the initiation and continuation of the said proceedings, the petitioner/accused No.5 has approached this Court seeking quashment.

Submissions on behalf of the Petitioner:
3.1.

Learned counsel for the petitioner contends that the petitioner has been falsely implicated and that the continuation of criminal proceedings against her amounts to a gross abuse of the process of law.
It is emphatically argued that a careful reading of the charge sheet discloses no independent or legally admissible material connecting the petitioner with the alleged offences.
The prosecution case against the petitioner rests solely on the alleged confessional statements of co- accused, which, in law, do not constitute substantive evidence.

It is further submitted that it is a well-settled principle that the confession of a co-accused is, at best, a weak piece of evidence and cannot form the sole basis for prosecution or conviction unless it is duly corroborated by independent and reliable evidence.

3.2. Learned counsel, placing reliance on Karan Talwar v. State of Tamil Nadu, 2024 INSC 1012,
submits that the Hon'ble Supreme Court has reiterated that, in the absence of independent incriminating material, the confession of a co-accused cannot justify the implication of another accused.

sentences.text: Further citing, R.P. Kapur v. State of Punjab, AIR 1960 SC 866, pleaded that the foundational principles governing the exercise of inherent powers for quashing criminal proceedings were laid down.

State of Telangana, Law Finder ID 2561216, and submits that, it has been consistently held that proceedings based solely on the statements of co-accused, in the absence of corroborative evidence, are liable to be quashed.

Accordingly, it is contended that, in the absence of legally admissible evidence, continuation of the proceedings would amount to harassment and misuse of the criminal law machinery.

Submissions of the Prosecution:
4.

Learned Additional Public Prosecutor, upon referring to the material on record, submits that the petitioner's name surfaced primarily on the basis of the confessional statement of accused No.1.

sentences.text: However, he fairly concedes that, as per the charge sheet, no independent material or documentary evidence has been collected during the investigation to establish the petitioner's involvement or any monetary transaction attributable to her.
5. I have carefully perused the material available on record.

Analysis and Conclusion:
6. At the outset, it is pertinent to note that the inherent powers of the High Court under Section 528 BNSS (analogous to Section 482 Cr.P.C.) are intended to prevent abuse of the process of any Court and to secure the ends of justice.

The contours of this jurisdiction have been authoritatively delineated in R.P. Kapur (supra), wherein it was held that criminal proceedings may be quashed where, the allegations, even if taken at face value, do not constitute any offence; there exists a legal bar to the institution or continuation of proceedings; or there is no legal evidence to support the prosecution case.
7.

Upon a careful examination of the charge sheet, it is evident that no independent material,
whether in the form of documentary evidence, recovery, financial trail, or witness statements, has been placed on record to connect the petitioner with the alleged offences.
The entire case against the petitioner rests solely upon the alleged confessional statements of co-accused.
8. The evidentiary value of such statements is well settled.

Under Section 30 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, a confession of a co- accused is not substantive evidence and can be used only as a corroborative circumstance, that too in the presence of independent evidence pointing towards guilt.
This principle has been reiterated by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Deepakbhai Jagdishchandra Patel v. State of Gujarat, (2019) 16 SCC 547, and Karan Talwar v. State of Tamil Nadu (supra).

entities.text: Deepakbhai Jagdishchandra Patel v. State of Gujarat, (2019) 16 SCC 547
entities.label: PRECEDENT

entities.text: Karan Talwar v. State of Tamil Nadu
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: This Court, in Perni Aneesha and Shashikanth Cherla (supra), has also consistently held that prosecution based solely on such confessions, without corroboration, is legally unsustainable.

9. In the present case, the absence of independent witness testimony implicating the petitioner;
documentary or financial evidence establishing receipt or handling of funds; and any recovery or material linking the petitioner to the alleged conspiracy, clearly demonstrates that the prosecution lacks foundational evidentiary support against the petitioner.
Subjecting the petitioner to trial in such circumstances would amount to a misuse of the criminal justice process and result in unwarranted prejudice.

10. In light of the settled legal principles and the material on record, this Court is of the considered view that the present case squarely falls within the category warranting exercise of inherent jurisdiction, as continuation of the proceedings would amount to an abuse of the process of the Court.
11. Accordingly, the Criminal Petition is allowed.

The proceedings against the petitioner/accused No.5 in C.C. No.350 of 2017 on the file of the XII Additional Chief Metropolitan Magistrate,
Hyderabad, are hereby quashed.
